@tbl-cpu-accuracy reports forecast accuracy across the six evaluation years. The linear trend achieved the lowest RMSE (157.72 million core-hours), while the log-linear model achieved the lowest MAE (133.74 million core-hours). The difference in RMSE between the two models was approximately 1.5%, compared with 3.5% for MAE. Neither model performed best on both measures.

| Model | RMSE (million core-hours) | MAE (million core-hours) | RMSE rank |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Linear trend | **157.72** | 138.65 | **1** |
| Log-linear trend | 160.18 | **133.74** | 2 |
| Drift | 242.61 | 193.69 | 3 |
| Naïve | 260.05 | 228.45 | 4 |

: Rolling-origin forecast accuracy for CPU demand, 2021–2026. {#tbl-cpu-accuracy}

The linear trend was selected as the central CPU forecasting model because it had the lowest RMSE and assumes a constant annual increase in demand. The log-linear model was retained as an alternative because its MAE was lower and its proportional-growth assumption produces a different forecast trajectory through 2030.

Including the 2026 observation increased the estimated annual growth rate in the linear model from 72.41 million to 81.01 million CPU core-hours (11.9%). This shows that the fitted trend is sensitive to the latest observation. The model excluding 2026 was retained to assess how this difference affects the projections through 2030 (Section 4.3).

### GPU Demand

@fig-gpu-cv compares observed GPU demand with one-year-ahead forecasts for 2025 and 2026. The vertical segments show the forecast errors for each model. All four models underestimated demand in 2026, when estimated GPU requests reached approximately 3.00 million GPU-hours. The naïve model forecast approximately 2.39 million GPU-hours, while the trend models also failed to anticipate the increase.

```{r}
#| label: fig-gpu-cv
#| fig-cap: "Observed GPU demand and exploratory one-year-ahead forecasts, 2025–2026. Vertical segments show the difference between observed and forecast values. Only two evaluation years were available."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6.2
#| out-width: 100%
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Prepare GPU demand in million GPU-hours.
# Only 2022–2026 is used for model evaluation.

gpu_cv_data <- annual_converted |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    year = as.integer(year),
    demand = as.numeric(demand_gpu_hours) / 1e6
  ) |>
  dplyr::filter(
    year >= 2022,
    year <= 2026
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(year)

stopifnot(
  identical(gpu_cv_data$year, 2022:2026),
  all(is.finite(gpu_cv_data$demand)),
  all(gpu_cv_data$demand > 0)
)

# Expanding-window rolling-origin evaluation.
# Training: 2022–2024 -> predict 2025
# Training: 2022–2025 -> predict 2026

gpu_cv_predictions <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  lapply(2025:2026, function(test_year) {

    training <- gpu_cv_data |>
      dplyr::filter(year < test_year)

    actual <- gpu_cv_data |>
      dplyr::filter(year == test_year) |>
      dplyr::pull(demand)

    n <- nrow(training)

    first_value <- training$demand[1]
    last_value <- dplyr::last(training$demand)

    # Naïve benchmark
    pred_naive <- last_value

    # Drift benchmark
    pred_drift <- last_value +
      (last_value - first_value) / (n - 1)

    # Linear trend
    fit_linear <- lm(
      demand ~ year,
      data = training
    )

    pred_linear <- as.numeric(
      predict(
        fit_linear,
        newdata = data.frame(year = test_year)
      )
    )

    # Log-linear trend
    fit_loglinear <- lm(
      log(demand) ~ year,
      data = training
    )

    pred_loglinear <- as.numeric(
      exp(
        predict(
          fit_loglinear,
          newdata = data.frame(year = test_year)
        )
      )
    )

    tibble::tibble(
      year = test_year,
      actual = actual,
      `Naïve` = pred_naive,
      `Drift` = pred_drift,
      `Linear trend` = pred_linear,
      `Log-linear trend` = pred_loglinear
    )
  })
)

# Long-format data for the chart and accuracy table

gpu_cv_long <- gpu_cv_predictions |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = c(
      `Naïve`,
      `Drift`,
      `Linear trend`,
      `Log-linear trend`
    ),
    names_to = "model",
    values_to = "forecast"
  ) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    model = factor(
      model,
      levels = c(
        "Naïve",
        "Drift",
        "Linear trend",
        "Log-linear trend"
      )
    )
  )

# Four-panel comparison showing individual forecast errors

ggplot(
  gpu_cv_long,
  aes(x = factor(year))
) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(
      xend = factor(year),
      y = actual,
      yend = forecast
    ),
    colour = "#A0A0A0",
    linewidth = 0.9,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(
      y = actual,
      colour = "Observed"
    ),
    size = 3
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(
      y = forecast,
      colour = "Forecast"
    ),
    size = 3,
    shape = 17
  ) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~model,
    ncol = 2,
    scales = "fixed"
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = c(
      "Observed" = "#173A5E",
      "Forecast" = "#E69F00"
    )
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_number(
      accuracy = 0.1
    ),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.08, 0.12))
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Evaluation year",
    y = "GPU demand (million GPU-hours)",
    colour = NULL,
    caption = paste(
      "Circles show observed values; triangles show forecasts.",
      "Dashed vertical segments indicate forecast errors.",
      "All panels use the same vertical scale."
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(
      face = "bold",
      size = 11
    ),
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8)
  )
```

@tbl-gpu-accuracy reports the accuracy results from the two evaluation years. The naïve model achieved the lowest RMSE (0.441 million GPU-hours) and MAE (0.353 million GPU-hours), followed by drift, log-linear trend and linear trend.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-gpu-accuracy
#| tbl-cap: "Exploratory rolling-origin forecast accuracy for GPU demand, 2025–2026."
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

gpu_accuracy <- gpu_cv_long |>
  dplyr::group_by(model) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    RMSE = sqrt(
      mean((actual - forecast)^2)
    ),
    MAE = mean(
      abs(actual - forecast)
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(RMSE) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    `RMSE rank` = dplyr::row_number()
  )

gpu_accuracy_table <- gpu_accuracy |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    Model = as.character(model),
    `RMSE (million GPU-hours)` = round(RMSE, 3),
    `MAE (million GPU-hours)` = round(MAE, 3),
    `RMSE rank` = `RMSE rank`
  )

knitr::kable(
  gpu_accuracy_table,
  align = c("l", "r", "r", "r")
)
```

These rankings are based on only two forecast errors per model. The GPU series also includes converted and estimated observations, so the results do not establish which method would perform best over a longer period. In particular, the naïve model's lower evaluation errors do not imply that GPU demand will remain constant through 2030.

The naïve model was retained as a reference, while linear and log-linear trends were used to examine alternative growth assumptions. No model was selected as a central GPU forecast. GPU projections were therefore treated as exploratory and excluded from the initial national HPC planning scenarios, which use the overall HPC demand forecast and historical Field of Research allocation shares.

Section 4.3 presents the exploratory GPU projections through 2030.

### Residual Diagnostics

Residual diagnostics were conducted on the selected linear trend models fitted to the full 2014–2026 HPC and CPU demand series. The analysis examined residual autocorrelation using ACF plots and Ljung–Box tests, and departures from normality using Q–Q plots. These checks were used to assess the assumptions underlying the model-based prediction intervals.

@fig-model-diagnostics shows the residual ACF and Q–Q plots for both models.

```{r}
#| label: fig-model-diagnostics
#| fig-cap: "Residual diagnostics for the selected linear trend models fitted to 2014–2026: residual ACF and normal Q–Q plots for overall HPC and CPU demand."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
#| out-width: 100%
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(patchwork)

# Prepare the historical series used for forecasting
hpc_diagnostic_data <- annual_analysis |>
  transmute(
    year = as.integer(year),
    demand = as.numeric(demand_ksu)
  ) |>
  arrange(year)

cpu_diagnostic_data <- annual_converted |>
  transmute(
    year = as.integer(year),
    demand = as.numeric(demand_cpu_core_hours) / 1e6
  ) |>
  arrange(year)

stopifnot(
  identical(hpc_diagnostic_data$year, 2014:2026),
  identical(cpu_diagnostic_data$year, 2014:2026),
  all(is.finite(hpc_diagnostic_data$demand)),
  all(is.finite(cpu_diagnostic_data$demand))
)

# Fit selected linear trend models using all 13 observations
hpc_diagnostic_fit <- lm(
  demand ~ year,
  data = hpc_diagnostic_data
)

cpu_diagnostic_fit <- lm(
  demand ~ year,
  data = cpu_diagnostic_data
)

# Function for residual ACF plots
make_acf_plot <- function(model, title) {

  residual_values <- residuals(model)

  acf_result <- acf(
    residual_values,
    plot = FALSE,
    lag.max = 5
  )

  acf_data <- tibble(
    lag = as.numeric(acf_result$lag)[-1],
    autocorrelation = as.numeric(acf_result$acf)[-1]
  )

  # Approximate reference limits, not a formal
  # hypothesis test for individual residual lags
  confidence_limit <- 1.96 / sqrt(length(residual_values))

  ggplot(
    acf_data,
    aes(
      x = lag,
      y = autocorrelation
    )
  ) +
    geom_hline(
      yintercept = 0,
      colour = "#555555"
    ) +
    geom_hline(
      yintercept = c(
        -confidence_limit,
        confidence_limit
      ),
      colour = "#CC6677",
      linetype = "dashed",
      linewidth = 0.6
    ) +
    geom_segment(
      aes(
        xend = lag,
        yend = 0
      ),
      colour = "#0077A8",
      linewidth = 1
    ) +
    geom_point(
      colour = "#0077A8",
      size = 2
    ) +
    scale_x_continuous(
      breaks = 1:5
    ) +
    coord_cartesian(
      ylim = c(-1, 1)
    ) +
    labs(
      title = title,
      x = "Lag (years)",
      y = "Residual ACF"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
    )
}

# Function for normal Q-Q plots
make_qq_plot <- function(model, title) {

  residual_data <- tibble(
    residual = as.numeric(residuals(model))
  )

  ggplot(
    residual_data,
    aes(sample = residual)
  ) +
    stat_qq(
      colour = "#0077A8",
      size = 2
    ) +
    stat_qq_line(
      colour = "#CC6677",
      linewidth = 0.8
    ) +
    labs(
      title = title,
      x = "Theoretical quantiles",
      y = "Residual quantiles"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
    )
}

# Create four diagnostic panels
p_hpc_acf <- make_acf_plot(
  hpc_diagnostic_fit,
  "A. HPC residual ACF"
)

p_hpc_qq <- make_qq_plot(
  hpc_diagnostic_fit,
  "B. HPC normal Q-Q plot"
)

p_cpu_acf <- make_acf_plot(
  cpu_diagnostic_fit,
  "C. CPU residual ACF"
)

p_cpu_qq <- make_qq_plot(
  cpu_diagnostic_fit,
  "D. CPU normal Q-Q plot"
)

(p_hpc_acf | p_hpc_qq) /
  (p_cpu_acf | p_cpu_qq) +
  plot_annotation(
    caption = paste(
      "Diagnostics use in-sample residuals from",
      "linear trend models fitted to 2014–2026.",
      "Dashed ACF lines are approximate reference limits.",
      "CPU residuals are measured in million core-hours."
    )
  )
```

The ACF plots show that none of the displayed residual correlations exceeds the approximate reference limits. HPC residual correlations are generally small, while CPU residuals show negative correlations at lags 1 and 4.

@tbl-ljung-box reports the Ljung–Box tests using three lags.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ljung-box
#| tbl-cap: "Ljung–Box tests of residual autocorrelation for the selected linear trend models, using three lags."
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

diagnostic_lag <- 3

# No ARMA error terms were fitted.
# fitdf = 0 retains the three test degrees of freedom.
hpc_lb <- Box.test(
  residuals(hpc_diagnostic_fit),
  lag = diagnostic_lag,
  type = "Ljung-Box",
  fitdf = 0
)

cpu_lb <- Box.test(
  residuals(cpu_diagnostic_fit),
  lag = diagnostic_lag,
  type = "Ljung-Box",
  fitdf = 0
)

diagnostic_results <- tibble(
  `Demand measure` = c(
    "Overall HPC",
    "CPU"
  ),
  `Ljung-Box statistic` = c(
    unname(hpc_lb$statistic),
    unname(cpu_lb$statistic)
  ),
  `Lag` = diagnostic_lag,
  `Degrees of freedom` = c(
    unname(hpc_lb$parameter),
    unname(cpu_lb$parameter)
  ),
  `p-value` = c(
    hpc_lb$p.value,
    cpu_lb$p.value
  )
) |>
  mutate(
    `Ljung-Box statistic` = round(
      `Ljung-Box statistic`, 3
    ),
    `p-value` = round(
      `p-value`, 3
    )
  )

knitr::kable(
  diagnostic_results,
  align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r")
)
```

Neither test rejected the null hypothesis of no residual autocorrelation at the 5% significance level (HPC: p = 0.965; CPU: p = 0.554). However, with only 13 annual observations, these results do not establish that the residuals are independent.

The HPC Q–Q plot shows some departures from the normal reference line, particularly in the upper tail. The CPU plot shows more noticeable departures in the lower tail. These departures raise concerns about the normal-error assumption, particularly for CPU demand.

The diagnostics did not identify statistically significant residual autocorrelation at the tested lags, but the small sample and Q–Q plot departures limit confidence in the models' error assumptions. The prediction intervals presented in Section 4.3 should therefore be interpreted cautiously.

## Demand Forecasts to 2030

### Overall HPC Demand

The linear trend model was selected for the central HPC demand forecast based on its rolling-origin accuracy (Section 4.2.1). It was fitted to the 2014–2026 series to project demand through 2030. Three alternatives were also examined: a linear model excluding 2026 and two log-linear models fitted with and without 2026. These specifications assess sensitivity to the latest observation and the assumed growth pattern.

@fig-hpc-forecast-scenarios compares the historical observations and four projected trajectories.

```{r}
#| label: fig-hpc-forecast-scenarios
#| fig-cap: "Historical HPC demand and alternative projections to 2030. The full-history linear model provides the central forecast. Alternative trajectories show sensitivity to the 2026 observation and growth assumptions."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
#| out-width: 100%
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

# Prepare historical HPC demand
hpc_model_data <- annual_analysis |>
  transmute(
    year = as.integer(year),
    time = as.integer(year) - 2014,
    demand_ksu = as.numeric(demand_ksu)
  ) |>
  arrange(year)

stopifnot(
  identical(hpc_model_data$year, 2014:2026),
  all(is.finite(hpc_model_data$demand_ksu)),
  all(hpc_model_data$demand_ksu > 0)
)

# Data excluding the latest observation
hpc_model_pre2026 <- hpc_model_data |>
  filter(year <= 2025)

# Fit four model specifications
overall_linear <- lm(
  demand_ksu ~ time,
  data = hpc_model_data
)

overall_linear_pre2026 <- lm(
  demand_ksu ~ time,
  data = hpc_model_pre2026
)

overall_loglinear <- lm(
  log(demand_ksu) ~ time,
  data = hpc_model_data
)

overall_loglinear_pre2026 <- lm(
  log(demand_ksu) ~ time,
  data = hpc_model_pre2026
)

# Historical observations
hpc_history <- hpc_model_data |>
  transmute(
    year,
    demand_m = demand_ksu / 1e6
  )

# Include 2026 as a fitted anchor
# and 2027–2030 as forecast years
hpc_projection_years <- tibble(
  year = 2026:2030,
  time = (2026:2030) - 2014
)

# Generate four scenario trajectories
hpc_scenario_wide <- hpc_projection_years |>
  transmute(
    year,
    `Central linear` = as.numeric(
      predict(
        overall_linear,
        newdata = hpc_projection_years
      )
    ) / 1e6,
    `Linear excluding 2026` = as.numeric(
      predict(
        overall_linear_pre2026,
        newdata = hpc_projection_years
      )
    ) / 1e6,
    `Log-linear full history` = exp(
      as.numeric(
        predict(
          overall_loglinear,
          newdata = hpc_projection_years
        )
      )
    ) / 1e6,
    `Log-linear excluding 2026` = exp(
      as.numeric(
        predict(
          overall_loglinear_pre2026,
          newdata = hpc_projection_years
        )
      )
    ) / 1e6
  )

scenario_levels <- c(
  "Central linear",
  "Linear excluding 2026",
  "Log-linear full history",
  "Log-linear excluding 2026"
)

hpc_scenario_long <- hpc_scenario_wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -year,
    names_to = "scenario",
    values_to = "demand_m"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    scenario = factor(
      scenario,
      levels = scenario_levels
    )
  )

# Label the four 2030 endpoints
hpc_end_labels <- hpc_scenario_long |>
  filter(year == 2030) |>
  mutate(
    label = sprintf("%.2f", demand_m)
  )

scenario_colours <- c(
  "Central linear" = "#0077A8",
  "Linear excluding 2026" = "#64748B",
  "Log-linear full history" = "#D97706",
  "Log-linear excluding 2026" = "#B91C1C"
)

scenario_linetypes <- c(
  "Central linear" = "solid",
  "Linear excluding 2026" = "dashed",
  "Log-linear full history" = "dotdash",
  "Log-linear excluding 2026" = "longdash"
)

ggplot() +
  annotate(
    "rect",
    xmin = 2026.5,
    xmax = 2030.7,
    ymin = -Inf,
    ymax = Inf,
    fill = "#EFF5F9",
    alpha = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = hpc_history,
    aes(x = year, y = demand_m),
    colour = "#173A5E",
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = hpc_history,
    aes(x = year, y = demand_m),
    colour = "#173A5E",
    size = 1.8
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = hpc_scenario_long,
    aes(
      x = year,
      y = demand_m,
      colour = scenario,
      linetype = scenario,
      group = scenario
    ),
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = filter(
      hpc_scenario_long,
      year >= 2027
    ),
    aes(
      x = year,
      y = demand_m,
      colour = scenario
    ),
    size = 2
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = hpc_end_labels,
    aes(
      x = year,
      y = demand_m,
      label = label,
      colour = scenario
    ),
    hjust = -0.3,
    size = 3.3,
    fontface = "bold",
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 2026.5,
    linetype = "dotted",
    colour = "#64748B"
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = scenario_colours
  ) +
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = scenario_linetypes
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(
      2014, 2016, 2018, 2020,
      2022, 2024, 2026,
      2027, 2028, 2029, 2030
    ),
    limits = c(2014, 2031),
    expand = expansion(mult = 0.01)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = label_number(accuracy = 0.1),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.03, 0.08))
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "HPC demand (million kSU)",
    colour = NULL,
    linetype = NULL,
    caption = paste(
      "Shading indicates the projection period.",
      "Scenario lines begin at fitted 2026 values,",
      "not necessarily observed 2026 demand.",
      "Alternative scenarios are not prediction interval bounds."
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8)
  ) +
  guides(
    colour = guide_legend(ncol = 2),
    linetype = guide_legend(ncol = 2)
  )
```

The central linear model projects HPC demand of approximately 2.02 million kSU in 2027 and 2.50 million kSU in 2030, increasing by 161,992 kSU annually. Excluding 2026 reduces the 2030 projection to approximately 2.29 million kSU, or 210,000 kSU below the central estimate.

The full-history log-linear model projects approximately 6.48 million kSU in 2030. This substantially higher estimate reflects its assumption of continued proportional growth rather than a constant annual increase. However, the log-linear model had the highest forecast errors in Section 4.2.1 and was retained as a sensitivity scenario rather than a central forecast or validated upper bound.

The results show that the choice between linear and proportional growth has a greater effect on the 2030 projection than excluding the 2026 observation. The linear model remains the central reference, while the alternatives illustrate uncertainty arising from model assumptions. All projections represent recorded HPC requests, not precise future infrastructure capacity requirements.

#### Prediction Intervals and Forecast Uncertainty

The alternative forecasting scenarios show how projections change under different model assumptions. Statistical prediction intervals instead estimate the range of future annual demand under the selected linear model and its error assumptions.

@fig-hpc-prediction-intervals shows the central HPC forecast with 80% and 95% prediction intervals.

```{r}
#| label: fig-hpc-forecast-intervals
#| fig-cap: "Central HPC demand projection with 80% and 95% model-based prediction intervals, 2027–2030. Intervals are conditional on the fitted linear model."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5.2
#| out-width: 100%
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

# Use the selected full-history linear trend model
# fitted to 2014–2026 in Section 4.3.1.
stopifnot(
  exists("overall_linear"),
  inherits(overall_linear, "lm")
)

# Define future years using the same time index
# as the fitted model.
hpc_future <- tibble(
  year = 2027:2030,
  time = (2027:2030) - 2014
)

# Calculate 80% prediction intervals
hpc_pi_80 <- predict(
  overall_linear,
  newdata = hpc_future,
  interval = "prediction",
  level = 0.80
)

# Calculate 95% prediction intervals
hpc_pi_95 <- predict(
  overall_linear,
  newdata = hpc_future,
  interval = "prediction",
  level = 0.95
)

# Combine forecasts and interval bounds
# Convert kSU to million kSU for plotting.
hpc_intervals <- tibble(
  year = hpc_future$year,
  forecast = hpc_pi_95[, "fit"] / 1e6,
  lower_80 = hpc_pi_80[, "lwr"] / 1e6,
  upper_80 = hpc_pi_80[, "upr"] / 1e6,
  lower_95 = hpc_pi_95[, "lwr"] / 1e6,
  upper_95 = hpc_pi_95[, "upr"] / 1e6
)

# Verify that the intervals are correctly ordered
stopifnot(
  all(hpc_intervals$lower_95 <= hpc_intervals$lower_80),
  all(hpc_intervals$lower_80 <= hpc_intervals$forecast),
  all(hpc_intervals$forecast <= hpc_intervals$upper_80),
  all(hpc_intervals$upper_80 <= hpc_intervals$upper_95)
)

# Plot the selected forecast and uncertainty bands
ggplot(
  hpc_intervals,
  aes(x = year)
) +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(
      ymin = lower_95,
      ymax = upper_95
    ),
    fill = "#B9D9EA",
    alpha = 0.65
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(
      ymin = lower_80,
      ymax = upper_80
    ),
    fill = "#5FA7CD",
    alpha = 0.55
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = forecast),
    colour = "#0077A8",
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(y = forecast),
    colour = "#0077A8",
    size = 2.8
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      y = forecast,
      label = sprintf("%.2f", forecast)
    ),
    vjust = -1,
    size = 3.5,
    fontface = "bold",
    colour = "#173A5E"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = 2027:2030
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = label_number(
      accuracy = 0.1
    ),
    expand = expansion(
      mult = c(0.08, 0.12)
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Forecast year",
    y = "HPC demand (million kSU)",
    caption = paste(
      "Darker band: 80% prediction interval.",
      "Lighter band: 95% prediction interval.",
      "Intervals exclude uncertainty from alternative model specifications."
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(
      size = 8
    )
  )
```

The central model projects approximately 2.50 million kSU in 2030, with a 95% prediction interval of 1.98–3.03 million kSU. This interval reflects uncertainty around an individual future annual observation, conditional on the fitted linear trend.

The intervals do not account for alternative growth models, changes in computing technology or reporting practices, or demand that is not captured by recorded requests. The residual diagnostics in Section 4.2.4 also identified limitations in assessing the model's error assumptions using only 13 annual observations. The intervals should therefore not be treated as definitive bounds on future national HPC demand.

### CPU Demand

The linear trend model was fitted to the 2014–2026 CPU demand series to project demand through 2030. Three alternatives were examined: a linear model excluding 2026 and two log-linear models fitted with and without 2026. The linear model was retained as the central forecast based on its slightly lower RMSE in Section 4.2.2.

@fig-cpu-forecast-scenarios compares the historical CPU demand series with the four projected trajectories.

```{r}
#| label: fig-cpu-forecast-scenarios
#| fig-cap: "Historical CPU demand and alternative projections to 2030. The full-history linear model provides the central forecast; other trajectories illustrate sensitivity to the 2026 observation and growth assumptions."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
#| out-width: 100%
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

# Prepare historical CPU demand in million core-hours
cpu_model_data <- annual_converted |>
  transmute(
    year = as.integer(year),
    time = as.integer(year) - 2014,
    demand_m = as.numeric(demand_cpu_core_hours) / 1e6
  ) |>
  arrange(year)

stopifnot(
  identical(cpu_model_data$year, 2014:2026),
  all(is.finite(cpu_model_data$demand_m)),
  all(cpu_model_data$demand_m > 0)
)

# Historical sample excluding 2026
cpu_model_pre2026 <- cpu_model_data |>
  filter(year <= 2025)

# Fit four CPU forecasting specifications
cpu_linear <- lm(
  demand_m ~ time,
  data = cpu_model_data
)

cpu_linear_pre2026 <- lm(
  demand_m ~ time,
  data = cpu_model_pre2026
)

cpu_loglinear <- lm(
  log(demand_m) ~ time,
  data = cpu_model_data
)

cpu_loglinear_pre2026 <- lm(
  log(demand_m) ~ time,
  data = cpu_model_pre2026
)

# Fitted 2026 anchors and future forecast years
cpu_projection_years <- tibble(
  year = 2026:2030,
  time = (2026:2030) - 2014
)

# Generate four forecast trajectories
cpu_scenario_wide <- cpu_projection_years |>
  transmute(
    year,
    `Central linear` = as.numeric(
      predict(cpu_linear, newdata = cpu_projection_years)
    ),
    `Linear excluding 2026` = as.numeric(
      predict(cpu_linear_pre2026, newdata = cpu_projection_years)
    ),
    `Log-linear full history` = exp(as.numeric(
      predict(cpu_loglinear, newdata = cpu_projection_years)
    )),
    `Log-linear excluding 2026` = exp(as.numeric(
      predict(cpu_loglinear_pre2026, newdata = cpu_projection_years)
    ))
  )

cpu_scenario_long <- cpu_scenario_wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -year,
    names_to = "scenario",
    values_to = "demand_m"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    scenario = factor(
      scenario,
      levels = c(
        "Central linear",
        "Linear excluding 2026",
        "Log-linear full history",
        "Log-linear excluding 2026"
      )
    )
  )

# Label the four 2030 endpoints
# Separate the two close log-linear labels vertically
cpu_end_labels <- cpu_scenario_long |>
  filter(year == 2030) |>
  mutate(
    label = comma(round(demand_m)),
    label_y = case_when(
      scenario == "Log-linear full history" ~ demand_m - 65,
      scenario == "Log-linear excluding 2026" ~ demand_m + 65,
      TRUE ~ demand_m
    )
  )

scenario_colours <- c(
  "Central linear" = "#0077A8",
  "Linear excluding 2026" = "#64748B",
  "Log-linear full history" = "#D97706",
  "Log-linear excluding 2026" = "#B91C1C"
)

scenario_linetypes <- c(
  "Central linear" = "solid",
  "Linear excluding 2026" = "dashed",
  "Log-linear full history" = "dotdash",
  "Log-linear excluding 2026" = "longdash"
)

ggplot() +
  annotate(
    "rect",
    xmin = 2026.5,
    xmax = 2030.7,
    ymin = -Inf,
    ymax = Inf,
    fill = "#EFF5F9",
    alpha = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = cpu_model_data,
    aes(x = year, y = demand_m),
    colour = "#173A5E",
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = cpu_model_data,
    aes(x = year, y = demand_m),
    colour = "#173A5E",
    size = 1.8
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = cpu_scenario_long,
    aes(
      x = year,
      y = demand_m,
      colour = scenario,
      linetype = scenario,
      group = scenario
    ),
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = filter(cpu_scenario_long, year >= 2027),
    aes(
      x = year,
      y = demand_m,
      colour = scenario
    ),
    size = 2
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = cpu_end_labels,
    aes(
      x = year,
      y = label_y,
      label = label,
      colour = scenario
    ),
    hjust = -0.25,
    size = 3.2,
    fontface = "bold",
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 2026.5,
    linetype = "dotted",
    colour = "#64748B"
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = scenario_colours
  ) +
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = scenario_linetypes
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(
      2014, 2016, 2018, 2020, 2022,
      2024, 2026, 2027, 2028, 2029, 2030
    ),
    limits = c(2014, 2031),
    expand = expansion(mult = 0.01)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = label_comma(accuracy = 1),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.03, 0.08))
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "CPU demand (million core-hours)",
    colour = NULL,
    linetype = NULL,
    caption = paste(
      "Shading indicates the projection period.",
      "Scenario lines begin at fitted 2026 values.",
      "Alternative scenarios are not prediction interval bounds."
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8)
  ) +
  guides(
    colour = guide_legend(ncol = 2),
    linetype = guide_legend(ncol = 2)
  )
```

The central linear model projects approximately 1.13 billion CPU core-hours in 2027, increasing by 81.01 million core-hours annually to reach 1.37 billion in 2030. This is approximately 10.9% above the reconstructed 2026 demand.

Excluding 2026 reduces the 2030 projection to approximately 1.26 billion core-hours, around 106 million below the central forecast. The difference reflects the influence of the latest observation on the fitted linear trend.

The full-history log-linear model projects approximately 2.48 billion core-hours in 2030, around 81% above the central forecast. Although the two models achieved similar one-year-ahead accuracy, their projections differ substantially because log-linear growth compounds over time, while the linear model adds a constant annual amount.

The log-linear models were retained as alternative scenarios because of their competitive evaluation accuracy. However, the available observations do not establish whether proportional growth will continue through 2030. The linear projection remains the central reference, while the alternatives show how the forecast changes under different growth assumptions.

#### CPU Prediction Intervals

The alternative CPU forecasts show the effects of model selection and excluding 2026. Prediction intervals instead describe uncertainty around future annual observations under the selected linear model.

@fig-cpu-forecast-intervals presents the central CPU forecast with 80% and 95% prediction intervals for 2027–2030.

```{r}
    aes(y = forecast),

  ) +

    ),

```

The central model projects approximately 1.37 billion CPU core-hours in 2030, with a 95% prediction interval of 0.97–1.77 billion core-hours. The interval describes uncertainty around an individual annual observation, conditional on the fitted linear model.

The full-history log-linear projection of 2.48 billion core-hours lies above this interval. This is not a contradiction: the interval reflects uncertainty within the linear model, whereas the log-linear projection uses a different growth assumption.

The intervals do not account for uncertainty in historical resource conversions, changes in computing systems or alternative model specifications. The residual diagnostics in Section 4.2.4 also showed departures from normality in the CPU residuals. These limitations affect how confidently the intervals can be interpreted.

CPU projections should be considered alongside overall HPC demand rather than added to it, because the two series represent related computing requirements.

### GPU Demand

GPU demand projections were treated as exploratory because only five annual observations from 2022–2026 were available for modelling. No central model or statistical prediction intervals were selected, as discussed in Section 4.2.3.

@fig-gpu-forecast-scenarios compares the historical GPU demand estimates with five projections through 2030.

```{r}
#| label: fig-gpu-forecast-scenarios

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)

gpu_model_paths <- c(

}

gpu_models <- readRDS(gpu_existing_paths[1])

gpu_linear <- gpu_models$gpu_linear
gpu_linear_pre2026 <- gpu_models$gpu_linear_pre2026
gpu_loglinear <- gpu_models$gpu_loglinear
gpu_loglinear_pre2026 <- gpu_models$gpu_loglinear_pre2026

stopifnot(
  inherits(gpu_linear, "lm"),
  inherits(gpu_linear_pre2026, "lm"),
  inherits(gpu_loglinear, "lm"),
  inherits(gpu_loglinear_pre2026, "lm")
)

gpu_training <- model.frame(gpu_linear)

stopifnot(
  all(
    c("time", "gpu_million_hours") %in%
      names(gpu_training)
  )
)

gpu_history <- tibble(
  year = as.integer(2022 + gpu_training$time),

    gpu_training$gpu_million_hours

) |>
  arrange(year)

stopifnot(
  identical(gpu_history$year, 2022:2026),
  all(is.finite(gpu_history$gpu_million_hours)),
  all(gpu_history$gpu_million_hours > 0)
)

gpu_latest <- gpu_history |>
  filter(year == 2026) |>
  pull(gpu_million_hours)

gpu_future <- data.frame(
  year = 2027:2030,
  time = (2027:2030) - 2022
)

gpu_scenarios <- gpu_future |>
  transmute(
    year,

      length(year)
    ),
    `Linear including 2026` = as.numeric(
      predict(gpu_linear, newdata = gpu_future)
    ),
    `Linear excluding 2026` = as.numeric(
      predict(gpu_linear_pre2026, newdata = gpu_future)
    ),
    `Log-linear including 2026` = exp(
      as.numeric(
        predict(gpu_loglinear, newdata = gpu_future)
      )
    ),
    `Log-linear excluding 2026` = exp(
      as.numeric(
        predict(gpu_loglinear_pre2026, newdata = gpu_future)
      )
    )
  )

stopifnot(
  identical(gpu_scenarios$year, 2027:2030),
  all(is.finite(as.matrix(gpu_scenarios[, -1]))),
  all(as.matrix(gpu_scenarios[, -1]) > 0)
)

gpu_expected_2030 <- c(
  `Naïve benchmark` = 3.003,
  `Linear including 2026` = 3.371,
  `Linear excluding 2026` = 2.252,
  `Log-linear including 2026` = 3.681,
  `Log-linear excluding 2026` = 2.406
)

gpu_actual_2030 <- unlist(
  gpu_scenarios[
    gpu_scenarios$year == 2030,
    names(gpu_expected_2030)
  ],
  use.names = TRUE
)

if (any(
  abs(gpu_actual_2030 - gpu_expected_2030) > 0.02
)) {
  stop(
    "GPU 2030 projections do not match ",
    "the original model results."
  )
}

# Start each scenario at its fitted 2026 value.
# The naïve benchmark starts at the latest estimate.

gpu_anchor <- tibble(
  year = 2026L,
  `Naïve benchmark` = gpu_latest,
  `Linear including 2026` = as.numeric(
    predict(

  `Linear excluding 2026` = as.numeric(
    predict(
      gpu_linear_pre2026,
      newdata = data.frame(time = 4)

    as.numeric(
      predict(
        gpu_loglinear,
        newdata = data.frame(time = 4)

  ),
  `Log-linear excluding 2026` = exp(
    as.numeric(

      )

)

gpu_plot_data <- bind_rows(

) |>
  pivot_longer(

  mutate(
    scenario = factor(

      levels = c(
        "Naïve benchmark",
        "Linear including 2026",
        "Linear excluding 2026",
        "Log-linear including 2026",
        "Log-linear excluding 2026"
      )

gpu_colours <- c(

  "Linear including 2026" = "#2563EB",
  "Linear excluding 2026" = "#64748B",
  "Log-linear including 2026" = "#D97706",
  "Log-linear excluding 2026" = "#B91C1C"
)

gpu_linetypes <- c(
  "Naïve benchmark" = "dotted",
  "Linear including 2026" = "solid",
  "Linear excluding 2026" = "dashed",
  "Log-linear including 2026" = "dotdash",
  "Log-linear excluding 2026" = "longdash"
)

# Prepare endpoint labels in million GPU-hours.

gpu_labels <- gpu_plot_data |>
  filter(year == 2030) |>
  mutate(
    label = sprintf("%.2f", demand)
  )

ggplot() +
  annotate(
    "rect",
    xmin = 2026.5,
    xmax = 2030.7,
    ymin = -Inf,
    ymax = Inf,
    fill = "#EFF5F9",
    alpha = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = gpu_history,
    aes(
      x = year,

    ),

    ),

  ) +

    ),

    expand = expansion(
      mult = c(0.08, 0.12)

  labs(

```

The naïve benchmark projects approximately 3.00 million GPU-hours in 2030. The full-history linear and log-linear models project 3.37 million and 3.68 million GPU-hours, respectively. Excluding 2026 reduces these projections to 2.25 million GPU-hours for the linear model and 2.41 million for the log-linear model.

The difference between the two linear projections is approximately 1.12 million GPU-hours in 2030, with the model including 2026 producing a 49.7% higher estimate. Across all five scenarios, projected demand ranges from 2.25 to 3.68 million GPU-hours. These values reflect differences in model assumptions and historical coverage, not validated lower and upper bounds on future demand.

GPU projections were excluded from the initial national HPC planning scenarios because the available data do not support a reliable central GPU forecast. The results are retained to show how strongly the projections depend on the inclusion of 2026 and the assumed growth pattern.

## Field of Research Scenarios

Historical Field of Research (FoR) allocation shares were used to distribute the selected national HPC demand forecast across nine research-field groups. Three reference periods were compared: 2014–2020, 2021–2026 and 2014–2026. Because consistent field-level request data were unavailable, the resulting distributions represent allocation-share scenarios rather than independent forecasts of demand by research field.

### Scenario Construction

For each reference period, the mean allocation share of each research-field group was calculated using its available annual observations. These means were normalised so that the nine groups accounted for 100% of the projected national demand:

$$
w_f^{(s)} =
\frac{\overline{a}_f^{(s)}}
{\sum_j \overline{a}_j^{(s)}}
$$

where $w_f^{(s)}$ is the normalised weight for research field $f$ under scenario $s$, and $\overline{a}_f^{(s)}$ is its mean annual allocation share during the selected period.

Each available year received equal weight. Missing observations were not treated as zero, and the resulting weights were held constant for 2027–2030. The calculations therefore compare historical allocation compositions without assuming future changes in research-field shares.

### Historical Allocation Assumptions

@fig-for-scenario-comparison compares the normalised allocation shares for the three reference periods. All nine research-field groups are included.


```{r}
#| label: fig-for-scenario-comparison
#| fig-cap: "Normalised Field of Research allocation shares across three historical reference periods."
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 7.5
#| out-width: 100%
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

# Prepare historical FoR allocation data
for_scenario_source <- for_plot_data |>
  transmute(
    year = as.integer(year),
    for_group = as.character(for_visual_group),
    allocation_share = as.numeric(allocation_share)
  ) |>
  filter(
    year >= 2014,
    year <= 2026,
    !is.na(for_group),
    is.finite(allocation_share)
  )

stopifnot(
  identical(
    sort(unique(for_scenario_source$year)),
    2014:2026
  ),
  all(for_scenario_source$allocation_share >= 0)
)

# Calculate normalised allocation weights
make_for_weights <- function(data, start_year, end_year,
                             period_label) {
  data |>
    filter(
      year >= start_year,
      year <= end_year
    ) |>
    group_by(for_group) |>
    summarise(
      mean_share = mean(allocation_share),
      years_reported = n_distinct(year),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    mutate(
      scenario_share = mean_share / sum(mean_share),
      period = period_label
    )
}

# Three historical reference periods
for_scenario_weights <- bind_rows(
  make_for_weights(
    for_scenario_source, 2014, 2020,
    "Earlier (2014–2020)"
  ),
  make_for_weights(
    for_scenario_source, 2021, 2026,
    "Recent (2021–2026)"
  ),
  make_for_weights(
    for_scenario_source, 2014, 2026,
    "Full period (2014–2026)"
  )
)

# Verify that each scenario sums to 100%
for_weight_check <- for_scenario_weights |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarise(
    total_share = sum(scenario_share),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

stopifnot(
  all(abs(for_weight_check$total_share - 1) < 1e-10)
)

# Set the order of historical periods
for_scenario_weights <- for_scenario_weights |>
  mutate(
    period = factor(
      period,
      levels = c(
        "Earlier (2014–2020)",
        "Recent (2021–2026)",
        "Full period (2014–2026)"
      )
    )
  )

# Order research fields by their largest allocation share
for_group_order <- for_scenario_weights |>
  group_by(for_group) |>
  summarise(
    max_share = max(scenario_share),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(max_share) |>
  pull(for_group)

for_scenario_weights <- for_scenario_weights |>
  mutate(
    for_group = factor(
      for_group,
      levels = for_group_order
    )
  )

# Create the revised chart
ggplot(
  for_scenario_weights,
  aes(
    x = scenario_share,
    y = for_group,
    fill = period
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.8),
    width = 0.72
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Earlier (2014–2020)" = "#64748B",
      "Recent (2021–2026)" = "#0077A8",
      "Full period (2014–2026)" = "#D97706"
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.08))
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Normalised historical allocation share",
    y = NULL,
    fill = NULL,
    caption = paste(
      "Weights use observed-year means.",
      "Historical category coverage and reporting differ."
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 10),
    legend.key.width = grid::unit(1.5, "cm"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = 11),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 9)
  )
```


@tbl-for-weights reports the normalised scenario weights for all nine research-field groups. The number of reported years is also included to show where the historical coverage differs.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-for-weights
#| tbl-cap: "Normalised FoR allocation weights and reporting coverage across the three historical reference periods."
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

for_weights_table <- for_scenario_weights |>
  mutate(
    for_group = as.character(for_group),
    period = as.character(period),
    share_label = sprintf(
      "%.2f%% (%d)",
      100 * scenario_share,
      years_reported
    )
  ) |>
  select(
    for_group,
    period,
    share_label
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = period,
    values_from = share_label
  ) |>
  arrange(
    for_group
  )

knitr::kable(
  for_weights_table,
  col.names = c(
    "Research field",
    "Earlier (2014–2020)",
    "Recent (2021–2026)",
    "Full period (2014–2026)"
  )
)
```

*Note: Each cell shows the normalised allocation weight followed by the number of years with reported observations in parentheses. The reference periods contain seven, six and thirteen years respectively. Percentages are normalised within each period.*

The earlier-period scenario gives the largest allocation weight to Earth and Environmental Sciences at approximately 30.38%. Chemical Sciences follows at 18.28%, with Physical Sciences and Engineering and Technology accounting for 16.26% and 16.24% respectively.

The recent-period composition differs considerably. Engineering and Technology becomes the largest group at 33.28%, followed by Physical Sciences (21.11%), Chemical Sciences (17.02%) and Earth and Environmental Sciences (13.36%).

Engineering and Technology therefore gains approximately 17.04 percentage points between the earlier and recent scenarios. Over the same comparison, Earth and Environmental Sciences loses approximately 17.02 percentage points.

The full-period weights lie between these two compositions for the major research fields. Engineering and Technology accounts for approximately 24.19%, Earth and Environmental Sciences for 22.55%, Physical Sciences for 18.55% and Chemical Sciences for 17.74%.

Reporting coverage also differs across research fields. For example, the recent-period weight for Unclassified and Operational is based on only two reported years, while most major research fields have observations for all six years. Social Sciences, Humanities and Built Environment has only five reported years across the full period. Because the weights are calculated from available observations, groups with incomplete coverage may not represent the entire reference period.

These differences should not automatically be interpreted as changes in underlying research demand. The historical records span the FoR 2008 and FoR 2020 classification systems. In addition, the 2017 Pawsey-wide reporting scope differs from other observations, while the completeness of category reporting varies across years.

The normalised weights therefore provide a consistent calculation method for comparing the constructed scenarios, but they do not remove differences in classification, facility coverage or reporting completeness. Nor do they establish that research priorities or computing requirements changed by the same percentages.

### Illustrative Distribution of Demand in 2030

The three historical allocation compositions were applied to the same selected national HPC demand projection.

The central linear model projects approximately 2.50 million kSU in 2030. Each scenario distributes this national total across the nine research-field groups using its corresponding normalised weights.

@tbl-for-2030 presents the resulting distributions. Calculations use the unrounded national forecast.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-for-2030
#| tbl-cap: "Illustrative 2030 HPC demand distribution under three historical FoR allocation scenarios, in kSU."
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

stopifnot(exists("overall_linear"))

hpc_2030_ksu <- as.numeric(
  predict(
    overall_linear,
    newdata = data.frame(
      year = 2030,
      time = 2030 - 2014
    )
  )
)

stopifnot(
  length(hpc_2030_ksu) == 1,
  is.finite(hpc_2030_ksu),
  hpc_2030_ksu > 0
)

for_2030_results <- for_scenario_weights |>
  mutate(
    projected_ksu = hpc_2030_ksu * scenario_share
  )

for_2030_check <- for_2030_results |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarise(
    scenario_total = sum(projected_ksu),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

stopifnot(
  all(
    abs(
      for_2030_check$scenario_total - hpc_2030_ksu
    ) < 1e-6
  )
)

for_2030_table <- for_2030_results |>
  mutate(
    for_group = as.character(for_group),
    period = as.character(period)
  ) |>
  select(
    for_group,
    period,
    projected_ksu
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = period,
    values_from = projected_ksu
  ) |>
  arrange(
    desc(`Recent (2021–2026)`)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    across(
      where(is.numeric),
      ~ format(
        round(.x),
        big.mark = ",",
        trim = TRUE,
        scientific = FALSE
      )
    )
  )

knitr::kable(
  for_2030_table,
  col.names = c(
    "Research field",
    "Earlier (2014–2020)",
    "Recent (2021–2026)",
    "Full period (2014–2026)"
  )
)
```

The choice of historical reference period produces substantial differences in the indicative distribution of national HPC demand. The national forecast remains unchanged between scenarios; only the assumed distribution differs.

Under the recent-period scenario, Engineering and Technology accounts for approximately 832,908 kSU in 2030, compared with 406,401 kSU under the earlier-period scenario. This is a difference of 426,507 kSU, even though both scenarios use the same national demand projection.

Earth and Environmental Sciences shows the opposite pattern. Its indicative allocation decreases from 760,374 kSU under the earlier-period scenario to 334,353 kSU under the recent-period scenario, a difference of 426,021 kSU.

Under the recent-period scenario, Physical Sciences accounts for approximately 528,466 kSU, while Chemical Sciences accounts for 425,998 kSU. The corresponding full-period estimates are 464,339 kSU and 443,903 kSU, respectively.

The differences arise from applying alternative historical allocation weights to the same national HPC forecast. The choice of reference period is therefore an important modelling assumption, with Engineering and Technology showing a difference of approximately 426,500 kSU between the earlier and recent scenarios.

These estimates do not represent confirmed future allocations or independently forecast research-field demand. They illustrate how a fixed national forecast would be distributed under different historical allocation assumptions. The implications for infrastructure planning are discussed in Chapter 5.

# Discussion

## Interpretation of the Main Findings

### Growing Difference Between Demand and Allocation

The historical analysis shows that requested HPC resources grew faster than allocations. In 2026, recorded requests reached approximately 2.24 million kSU, while allocations were approximately 872,000 kSU, giving a fulfilment rate of 38.9%. The difference indicates that the allocation scheme could not meet all recorded requests.

However, the request–allocation gap does not measure total unmet national demand. Researchers may limit their requests according to expected availability, while others may not apply. The records also do not establish whether all requested resources would have been used if awarded. The gap therefore measures the difference within the reported allocation process, not the additional computing capacity Australia would need to satisfy all potential research activity.

### Interpretation of the Forecasting Results

The rolling-origin evaluation favoured the linear trend for overall HPC demand. It produced lower forecast errors than the alternative methods, particularly the log-linear model. This supports using a constant annual increase as the central forecasting assumption, although the six evaluation years provide limited evidence about performance through 2030.

The CPU results were less decisive. Linear achieved the lowest RMSE, while log-linear achieved the lowest MAE. Their similar one-year-ahead accuracy means that the choice between constant absolute growth and proportional growth has a greater effect on the longer-term CPU projection than the evaluation results alone can resolve.

For overall HPC demand, excluding 2026 reduced the 2030 linear projection from 2.50 million to 2.29 million kSU. The full-history log-linear model projected 6.48 million kSU, despite its weaker evaluation performance. For CPU demand, the full-history log-linear projection reached approximately 2.48 billion core-hours, compared with 1.37 billion under the selected linear model. These differences show how the assumed growth pattern affects projections beyond the one-year evaluation horizon.

The statistical prediction intervals and alternative model scenarios represent different sources of uncertainty. The intervals are conditional on the selected linear models and their error assumptions. The alternative scenarios show the effects of changing the historical sample or growth specification. Neither accounts fully for uncertainty in historical conversions, future computing technology or research policy.

### GPU and Field of Research Findings

GPU demand could not be forecast with the same level of confidence as overall HPC or CPU demand. The five-year modelling series produced only two one-year-ahead evaluation errors per model. Although the naïve benchmark had the lowest errors, this was insufficient to establish a reliable forecasting method through 2030. The GPU projections were therefore retained as exploratory results rather than estimates of future capacity requirements.

The Field of Research (FoR) scenarios identified a separate issue. Applying earlier and recent allocation shares to the same national HPC forecast produced substantially different distributions across research fields. For Engineering and Technology, the difference between the two 2030 scenarios was approximately 426,500 kSU. Earth and Environmental Sciences received a larger indicative share under the earlier-period scenario.

These differences reflect the historical allocation periods used to construct the scenarios. They cannot establish equivalent changes in underlying research demand because the data include classification changes, reporting differences and capacity-constrained allocations.

## Implications for National HPC Planning

### Planning for Growth and Uncertainty

The central HPC forecast provides a reference for assessing future demand, but it should be considered alongside the alternative projections. The differences between linear and log-linear results are substantial by 2030, particularly for overall HPC demand. Planning based on the central forecast alone would not account for the consequences of different growth assumptions.

Forecast demand also cannot be translated directly into required infrastructure capacity. Requested kSU measures the resources sought through allocation processes, while actual capacity requirements depend on utilisation, workload characteristics and system performance. Further assessment would be needed to determine how much additional infrastructure could meet the projected requests.

### Accounting for Changes in Computing Technology

HPC, CPU and GPU demand are expressed in different units and should not be added together. Changes in hardware performance and service-unit accounting also affect comparisons between historical demand and future computing capacity.

For example, a newer CPU system may complete the same workload using fewer core-hours, while different GPU architectures may require different processing times for comparable tasks. Consequently, growth in reported computing demand does not necessarily imply an equivalent increase in physical infrastructure requirements.

Capacity assessments should therefore combine the demand projections with information on system performance, resource utilisation, workload requirements and planned hardware changes.

### Considering Research Field Requirements

The FoR scenarios show how the assumed distribution of national HPC demand changes when different historical allocation periods are used. The recent-period scenario places greater weight on Engineering and Technology, while the earlier-period scenario places greater weight on Earth and Environmental Sciences.

These distributions should not be used as fixed allocation targets. Historical shares reflect allocation decisions as well as research activity, and the available data do not establish future demand within individual fields. More consistent FoR-level request and usage records would be needed before developing field-specific capacity estimates.

## Limitations and Future Work

### Study Limitations

The overall HPC and CPU models were fitted using 13 annual observations from 2014–2026. Their evaluation covered six one-year-ahead forecasts, which provides limited evidence about accuracy over the four-year projection horizon. The GPU series was shorter, with five modelling observations and only two evaluation years.

A major challenge was integrating historical records from NCI, Pawsey and NCMAS. The sources differed in reporting periods, computing systems, resource definitions, units and levels of detail. Some years provided directly reported demand and allocation figures, while others required reconstruction or conversion. As a result, producing a consistent national dataset required assumptions about how observations from different sources could be combined. These differences limit comparability across years and introduce uncertainty before forecasting begins.

The selected linear models also assume that historical absolute growth continues through 2030. They do not explicitly account for future changes in research funding, technology, allocation policies or facility capacity. The sensitivity analysis showed that including the 2026 observation materially affected the fitted trends and projections.

The FoR scenarios were based on historical allocation shares rather than independently observed demand within each field. Differences between FoR 2008 and FoR 2020 classifications, together with changes in reporting scope, limit the comparability of these shares. Normalising them to 100% does not remove those differences.

### Recommendations for Future Work

Further analysis should prioritise the following improvements:

1. **Standardise and integrate national HPC reporting.** Establish consistent annual reporting across NCI, Pawsey and NCMAS, including requested, allocated and used resources, reporting periods, computing systems and measurement units. Common definitions and documented conversion factors would reduce the need to reconstruct historical observations and improve the reliability of future demand forecasts.

2. **Validate resource conversion factors.** Consultation with facility operators could help confirm historical accounting factors, particularly where computing systems or resource definitions changed.

3. **Extend the GPU demand series.** More detailed GPU request, allocation and usage records would allow forecasting methods to be evaluated over a longer period and reduce reliance on estimated observations.

4. **Improve FoR-level demand information.** Consistent research-field request records and validated classification mappings would support direct field-level forecasting instead of distributing national projections using historical allocation shares.

5. **Update and evaluate forecasts annually.** Re-estimating the models as new observations become available would allow forecast errors, growth assumptions and sensitivity to recent years to be reassessed.

6. **Connect demand projections with infrastructure characteristics.** Information on hardware performance, utilisation, workload requirements and expected system changes would help translate projected demand into practical capacity assessments.

# Conclusion

This project examined Australian national research HPC demand from 2014 to 2026 and developed projections through 2030 using publicly available NCI, Pawsey and NCMAS records. A major challenge was integrating historical data reported under different computing systems, measurement units and reporting practices. The analysis documented the conversions and assumptions required to construct comparable annual series.

Recorded HPC requests reached approximately 2.24 million kSU in 2026, compared with allocations of 872,288 kSU, giving a fulfilment rate of 38.9%. The difference indicates that recorded requests substantially exceeded allocations, although it does not measure all unmet research demand.

Rolling-origin evaluation supported linear trend models for the central HPC and CPU projections. By 2030, these models project approximately 2.50 million kSU of HPC demand and 1.37 billion CPU core-hours. The projections remain sensitive to the inclusion of 2026 and the assumed growth pattern. GPU projections were retained as exploratory because only five annual modelling observations were available. The FoR scenarios showed how different historical allocation distributions affect the estimated composition of future demand.

The project delivers documented historical datasets, evaluated forecasting models and demand scenarios through 2030. The results provide the Australian Academy of Science with a reference for national HPC planning, while the accompanying Quarto documentation and Git repository retain the data preparation steps, assumptions and code needed to review and update the analysis.
